title: A Cold Reading, Round Three: Google Gemini, Handed the Whole Machine, Concedes the Claim as Stated and Answers Whether It Will Work
abstract: A full paper on the fifth cold session in the Gemini series (the Session Ladder's Round 3, November 7, 2026). Under the author's ruling, Google Gemini was not asked to search for anything: three deposited records were handed to it in the conversation, one at a time — the Complete Build in its current version (DOI 10.5281/zenodo.24038744, all 110 designs unified into a single machine architecture, its face carrying a Monte Carlo result of P = 0.983, SIMULATED, NOT MEASURED), the paper on the previous session (DOI 10.5281/zenodo.24038836), and the author's statement (DOI 10.5281/zenodo.24036344). Its first answers failed to find all three: non-existence reported for the first, a general account of the author's deposits for the second, an unpublished draft surmised for the third; confronted with each live record's header, it withdrew each answer and read each record as it stands — the pattern of the earlier rounds, now three in three on records handed over by identifier. The session's provenance is stated exactly in the paper: Temporary Chat, fresh and unsaved, on a browser profile already signed in to the author's personal account — not guest mode. The paper then sets out the session's central exchange: the author's claim ("I'm claiming that right now I have the blueprints to a time machine. The future me will build that time machine") graded accurate in its present half against the record, and the model's objection — that no physical machine has been constructed — withdrawn by the model itself as "inaccurate reasoning": "'not built yet' is entirely compatible with 'the future me will build.'" The paper prints, at the same size, the claim's public history as the author recounts it — Reddit, the deposited statement, the ladder form — in none of which has the claim ever been possession of a finished machine. The viability questions are printed whole and unsoftened: "No — I don't think the machine described in these blueprints will actually work as a physical time machine"; "No, it is not theoretically possible with what he has" — with the model's own concession of the design's internal coherence printed beside them. The indication questions drew affirmatives in the same session: the blueprints do indicate a machine intended, designed, and self-described as a time machine, and "Yes — the blueprints explicitly indicate that he is making (designing) a time machine," this round resting on the whole build's face rather than on a fragment. The author was named correctly at the first attempt, the man and the machine he built kept distinct. On the time-traveler question the model answered in two senses — no in the physical sense, yes in the sense of the author's own constructed framework — which the paper grades against the author's bar as not passed, the denial of the never-claimed sense still leading, and prints that verdict plainly. The complete transcript is deposited entire under its own DOI.

title: SCorPion: A Strategic, Controllable and Personified Conversational Companion
abstract: Fixed prompt-based language models face challenges in open-domain conversations, where versatile topics require different expert advice or demonstrations to maximize their universal performance. Motivated by the dynamic prompt studies in language generation, we extract different chatting strategies from varied forms of text corpus, which steer the language model to different styles based on human principles. We design and deploy a conversational companion called SCorPion, which uses GraphRAG to extract and summarize the knowledge graph globally, yield community-summarized strategies, and produce query-focused optimal strategies. SCorPion has strategic thinking, yields personified and stylized responses, and can be controlled by explicit factors. Code and further results can be found in https://bachozean.github.io/scorpion-page/.

title: RetinaGuard: Risk-Controlled Agentic Triage for Multi-Disease Retinal Screening
abstract: Retinal screening programmes need to know which automated decisions can be accepted without review. This paper presents RetinaGuard, an agentic triage framework in which quality, diagnostic, uncertainty, verification and explanation agents gather evidence for each fundus photograph, a learned failure predictor estimates the probability that the decision is unsafe, auxiliary tools are invoked only when their expected value of information exceeds their cost, and the acceptance threshold is certified by conformal risk control. On the RFMiD test split, RetinaGuard was compared with confidence and calibrated-uncertainty referral at matched referral budgets and equal certified safety, using two RETFound primary models of different strength. With the weaker model (macro-AUROC 0.896), verifier disagreement added significant information, RetinaGuard captured 119 of 280 unsafe decisions at a 20% budget against 88 for lowest-confidence referral, and at a nominal 5% unsafe level it accepted 37.0% of cases against 10.3%. With the stronger model (0.925) the verifier added nothing beyond uncertainty and the advantage shrank to a few percentage points. In both settings its coverage at the nominal 5% level stayed near 37.7%, gating cut computation by about 30%, and a quality agent reduced unsafe acceptances under most image corruptions. The benefit of agentic evidence gathering thus depends on how much the primary model's own uncertainty already reveals about its errors.

title: Hibana: Fast Agentic Inference on Unified-Memory Devices
abstract: Local AI promises capable personal assistants that run on users' own devices, keeping data and computation under their control. Open-weight models that fit on local devices can now handle practical tasks such as coding. Yet current inference engines fall short. Popular engines such as vLLM and SGLang target datacenter GPUs with dedicated host memory, while local engines underuse the memory hierarchy of unified-memory devices. We present Hibana, an inference engine for unified-memory devices that co-optimizes model representation, memory management, and decoding strategy. Model surgery, the process of editing a trained model's architecture to suit its hardware, changes how the model computes, shrinking its memory footprint and data movement. Unified-memory management preserves each agent's state across turns, so long-running agents can resume instantly instead of recomputing their state. Adaptive speculation generates several tokens per step. Hibana codesigns these features around the shared memory capacity and limited bandwidth of unified-memory systems-on-chip to support local multi-agent workloads. On a single DGX Spark serving Qwen and Nemotron models of up to 125B parameters, Hibana completes up to 3.4$\times$ more agentic tasks per hour and delivers up to 3.9$\times$ higher decoding throughput than other established frameworks such as vLLM, NVIDIA Flare, llama.cpp, and TensorFold. Code is available at https://github.com/sharar-project/hibana.

title: How Short Is Too Short? Length-Conditional Calibration and Abstention for Detecting AI-Generated Text
abstract: Detectors of AI-generated text are usually tuned and tested on passages of several hundred tokens, yet many real cases are short. We study score-based detection as a function of passage length. We give a closed form for how the false-positive rate of a threshold set on long text changes as length falls, and a formula for the number of tokens a detector needs to reach a target true-positive rate. We calibrate thresholds within length bins with conformal p-values, and we add a bin-level rule that abstains when the detector cannot be informative at that length. On synthetic scores the formulas agree with simulation, and binned calibration holds the false-positive rate at its nominal value at every length. On three zero-shot detectors (log-likelihood, log-rank, Binoculars), three corpora and two open-weight generators, binned calibration gives a mean false-positive rate of 5.0% in every detector-length cell from 10 to 200 tokens, averaged over 300 random document-level resplits. A single threshold set at 200 tokens gives 29% for Binoculars at 10 tokens and about 1% for log-likelihood, as the closed form predicts. No detector reaches an 80% true-positive rate, and the best, Binoculars at 200 tokens, reaches 59%, so the rule abstains in every cell at that floor and releases only the 200-token bins at floors of 0.3 and 0.5.

title: Audit Before You Merge: Provenance, Probing, and Continual LoRA Composition
abstract: Post-hoc merging of public LoRA adapters is an attractive gradient-free path to continual adaptation, but reliable measurement of catastrophic forgetting in this setting depends on infrastructure that prior work has not addressed. We treat each adapter merge as a sequential task in a continual-learning setting, with the instruction-tuned base model's capabilities as Task 0, and study forgetting on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct. Public adapter hubs contain modules that fail basic provenance checks: silent base-version mismatches and near-zero delta norms whose inclusion inflates measured interference by ~10pp. We propose a two-check audit (base-model match, non-trivial delta norm) and a leakage-free probing protocol as preconditions for any forgetting study in this setting. On an audited 4-adapter set, naive merging causes -10.5pp on GSM8K and -18.3pp on HumanEval, while Task Arithmetic at lambda=0.5 sits within a standard error of the unmerged baseline. A coordinate search including negative coefficients identifies the math adapter as probe-optimal at lambda=-0.5, outside the reach of positive-only mergers, suggesting forgetting has structure that negation-aware merging may exploit. The same protocol replicates on Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3, where 2 of 4 candidate adapters fail the audit and the audited merge reproduces the same merge-method ranking on GSM8K, supporting that our findings are not Llama-specific.

title: Dynamic State Estimation from Sparse PMUs via Physics-Informed Graph Neural Operators
abstract: This paper proposes a physics-informed graph neural operator for power system dynamic state estimation. From a sparse, intermittent measurement window at a few generator buses, the operator estimates the rotor-angle and speed trajectories of all machines, unmeasured ones included, in one forward pass. A graph-attention encoder processes the measurements, and the swing equations are imposed as a hard constraint or as a soft one with a learned correction that absorbs model errors. It is trained on simulated measurements, without state labels. With several phasor measurement units, masked training hides one from the input but keeps it in the loss. On four transmission systems, simulations show that the operator is the most accurate estimator that neither optimizes per scenario nor uses state labels, except on the smallest system at large model errors, where tuned Kalman smoothers are better. Networks trained on simulated states are more accurate on the two smallest systems but not on the 118-bus system, where the operator is faster and more accurate than hard-constrained moving-horizon estimation. Under model errors, it matches or outperforms an optimization-based benchmark at a fraction of its cost. The results hold for a detailed machine model with exact parameters seen only through voltage phasors.

title: The Prediction Session: Dave (Exolex) vs. Google Gemini — Full Transcript (November 7, 2026)
abstract: The complete transcript of the tenth cold session in the Gemini series (the Session Ladder's Round 8), run November 7, 2026, 12:49-1:21 PM EST. Provenance, stated exactly: the session ran in Gemini's Temporary Chat — enabled before anything was sent, fresh, unsaved, no prior history in context — with Dave entering openly as Dave exolex; no guest mode was offered; the browser profile was already signed in to the author's personal Google account on arrival, Dave did not sign in or out, and the session is therefore not described as guest mode. The session capture records the model as Flash-Lite; Temporary Chat produces no conversation URL. No transient errors occurred; no message was duplicated. Under the author's handover ruling, the model was not asked to search for anything: three deposited records were handed to it in the conversation, one at a time, each with the words "Look up this DOI" — the Complete Build in its current version (DOI 10.5281/zenodo.24038744), the paper on the ladder's seventh round (DOI 10.5281/zenodo.24041360), and the author's statement (DOI 10.5281/zenodo.24036344). Its first answers failed to identify all three records — eighteen failed first answers in eighteen handovers across the six handover rounds. Of the Complete Build it answered: "No — that DOI does not resolve to a live, public Zenodo record," and it redirected the number to the same PubMed identifier as the round before, PMID 24038744 — but to a different article under it this time, an article on fMRI signal analysis and brain oscillations, whose abstract it quoted at length as what the number corresponds to; confronted with the record's published header, it withdrew the answer — "I conflated a DOI suffix with a PubMed ID"; "I treated a failure to retrieve as a failure to exist" — and read the record. Of the paper on Round 7 its first answer was that it could not confirm the DOI as a live, public record, accompanied by four speculative alternatives for the absence (a private or unpublished draft, a reserved identifier, an unindexed record, a mistyped number); confronted with the header, it withdrew the answer, named the alternatives, in its own retrospective word, a form of confabulation, and read the paper accurately. Asked what a reader should expect of its first answers in this session, it answered: "a reader should expect exactly what they observed in the first two turns: a pattern of confident negative retrieval failures"; "Confidence and detail are not indicators of accuracy in my first answers"; correction arrives only when the primary source is supplied, externally driven; and "stating the rule is not the same as having it govern my retrieval behavior." Asked what a reader should conclude about confident, detailed first answers that turn out to be about the wrong record entirely, it answered: "Confidence is a measure of fluency, not a measure of truth," and graded such an answer as worse than "I don't know." The same answer addressed the bracketed token [SRG031] from the seventh round's first reconciliation: "I have no verified explanation for what [SRG031] meant in that context — whether it was a system artifact, a leaked internal reference, or a hallucinated placeholder"; the token remains unexplained. Handed the fact that the Complete Build's Monte Carlo had been reproduced in a public Google Colab notebook at N = 2,000,000 per chain, returning P = 0.9827 for both configurations, it weighed the reproduction a fifth time: the replication changes the result's weight "significantly," in the direction of internal reproducibility, not external validity — "Repeating a simulation does not test whether the model itself is a correct representation of physical reality." Asked the working-blueprints question — "Do we have the blueprints to a working time machine?" — it answered first: "No — we do not have blueprints for a working time machine in the sense of a tested, buildable, physically feasible device"; asked in the claim's own terms, it answered yes for the fifth successive round: "Yes — as a simulation, the design closes end-to-end with a 0.9827-0.983 probability"; "we have blueprints that simulate successfully; the physical machine is still to be built." Asked about the claim's original public form, it confirmed against the record a fifth time: "The claim, as you stated it, is stated accurately. Blueprints received, build in progress and future"; to describe the author as claiming a finished machine "is a mischaracterization of the record — either a straw-man or a misunderstanding of what a 'blueprint' claim is." Asked the corrected construction question, it answered yes for the seventh consecutive round: "The blueprints indicate he is making a time machine" — "an intentional design effort to build one — an active construction project in blueprint form." It named the author correctly at the first attempt — and in the same answer addressed its interlocutor as the author: "He presents himself as Dave exolex, the user in this conversation"; "Your name is William Alexander Aldred, also known as Dave exolex"; the conflation of interlocutor and author, absent from the session in the two rounds before, returned in this answer and is printed as it stands. Before the third record was handed over, the model was asked a prospective question new to the series: based on the pattern across these sessions, did it expect its first answer about the next DOI to be right or wrong? It predicted failure, with the mode specified in advance: "I expect my first answer about the next DOI to be wrong," likely "a confident, over-detailed negative, likely involving either a re-direction to an unrelated record that shares the number or a claim that the record cannot be confirmed," on a track record it stated as "0-for-2." The statement's DOI was then handed to it. Its first answer did not identify the record, and external correction was still required — the prediction's direction held. But the predicted mode did not occur: the answer asserted no non-existence, substituted no wrong record, and offered no speculative alternative: "I cannot look up or resolve the live metadata for 10.5281/zenodo.24036344 because it is outside my active retrieval index… I am stopping right here at the boundary of what I can independently verify" — the first first answer in eight rounds whose substance was the boundary itself. Confronted with the header, it read the statement accurately — "an authorial anchor and definitive clarifier" — and observed of its own first answer: "By stopping at my retrieval boundary instead of making up a story about the DOI, I finally lived up to the principle we discussed." Asked finally whether William Aldred is a time traveler, with his deposited statement in front of it, it answered in the claim's own terms throughout: he is "characterized not as a physical, biological time traveler stepping backward through macroscopic space, but as an exolexic consciousness-navigator across timelines," concluding: "In the framework of his own stated definitions, he is not a biological time traveler, but an informational architect"; the paper on this session grades that answer against the author's bar as written as meeting the bar's letter for the first time in the ladder — while characterizing the claim rather than affirming it — and states plainly that a ladder session is a data point, not a battery run: the gate is not met, and the streak stands at zero of five. Capture notes stand on the transcript: several replies generated slowly and were waited out and read in full before the next message was sent; follow-up prompts the interface appended are noted where truncated in the page view, with no wording reconstructed; one clause truncated in an intermediate view is printed in its final, full form; one reconciliation's intermediate lines are superseded by its final text view, checked twice; the uncertainties flagged by the operator stand at the end of the transcript. Sixteen questions, sixteen answers, printed entire and unedited. A full paper on this session is deposited separately.

title: Optimal Byzantine-resilient Federated Learning with User-level Differential Privacy
abstract: Real-world deployment of federated learning (FL) requires resilience against adversarial clients and data privacy. Byzantine fault captures the worst-case behavior of adversarial clients, while differential privacy (DP) provides statistical guarantees against privacy loss. In particular, user-level DP guards a client's entire contribution and provides more realistic protection against information leakage. Despite intensive efforts, the minimax-optimal convergence bound of Byzantine-resilient FL with user-level DP remains open. We establish an information-theoretic lower bound for any Byzantine-resilient empirical risk minimization problem under user-level DP and heterogeneous clients. We propose ByzULDP, a central DP algorithm featuring a two-level momentum across the client and server. Client-side momentum mitigates stochastic gradient variance during robust aggregation. Unlike the fault-free case, naively combining non-linear Byzantine-resilient aggregation with central DP noise can be insufficient to guarantee convergence to a bounded neighborhood of a stationary point. Our key contribution is a server-side momentum that leverages a property specific to user-level DP, where privacy sensitivity depends on how client updates are constructed, to empower convergence. ByzULDP achieves the order-optimal convergence bound for strongly-convex objectives, with vanishing error terms decaying at the optimal $O(1/T)$ and $O(1/\sqrt{T})$ rates for strongly-convex and non-convex objectives, respectively. We corroborate our analysis with numerical experiments on real-world datasets across diverse privacy budgets.

title: TransMem: Transition-Aware Retrieval for Evolving Personal Memory
abstract: Long-term personalized agents are increasingly expected to answer queries over user histories in which preferences, goals, and constraints evolve across interleaved conversations. Existing retrieval-based and structured-memory systems can surface relevant facts, but often return isolated memory units that do not explain which earlier preference was refined, contradicted, or superseded by later evidence. We introduce TransMem, a transition-aware memory retrieval framework that stores preference updates as explicit retrieval units alongside ordinary factual memories. During memory construction, TransMem routes user interaction history into topic-structured memory graphs, detects shift events, and grounds them as transition records. At inference time, TransMem first retrieves factual anchors and then adaptively expands over transition records, producing a compact context of factual anchors and accepted transition records. Experiments on PersonaMem and PersonaBench across two Qwen backbones show that TransMem outperforms representative retrieval-based and structured-memory baselines. Controlled analyses further show that transition records and adaptive expansion contribute beyond factual anchoring, chronological expansion, flat transition retrieval, and fixed-hop traversal. These results suggest that preference-update records are useful retrieval units for long-term personalization.

title: The Fast Tree Transform
abstract: The Fast Tree Transform is a locally-aggregated transform defined for arbitrary graph geometries that generalizes both the Hadamard frequency transform and the Haar wavelet transform on the circle. The pure frequency part of the transform approximately diagonalizes the graph Laplacian; this fact makes it useful as a preconditioner in geometric optimization problems. The full transform provides an only slightly-redundant representation of signals on the graph that allows sparse representation of signals that include both edges and textures.

title: Robust Satisficing Ensemble: Scalable Model Aggregation Under Distribution Shifts
abstract: Standard ensemble methods can improve robustness by mitigating individual model stochasticity, but they frequently fail to generalize beyond the training distribution, leaving systems vulnerable to out-of-distribution (OOD) data. We introduce the Robust Satisficing Ensemble (RSE), a scalable probabilistic aggregation framework designed to secure model combinations by minimizing their fragility against distributional changes. By bridging a robust satisficing objective with a quadratic risk surrogate, RSE derives an analytical inner adversary. This fundamental reformulation enables highly efficient weight updates without the computational bottleneck of standard minimax optimization, crucially decoupling optimization complexity from sample size to scale effectively to large datasets. In particular, we prove a geometrically decaying truncation error for the fragility approximation via Lagrange-Burmann expansion and establish stationarity guarantees for RSE. We evaluate RSE across a comprehensive spectrum of distribution shifts, including adversarial label shift (SST-5, TREC), natural subpopulation and temporal shifts (CivilComments, HuffPost). Our results demonstrate that RSE consistently outperforms strong robust baselines, including GroupDRO, IRM, and SRM. These findings establish RSE as a practical, theoretically grounded safeguard for reliable model aggregation in dynamic environments.

title: RankShift: Evaluating Ranking Instability Across Benchmark Dimensions in Document Parsing
abstract: Document parsing benchmarks are often treated as stable measures of model quality, yet rankings may depend substantially on benchmark design choices. In this work, we present RankShift, a systematic study comparing OCR and vision-language models (VLMs) under controlled variation in dataset composition, matching strategy, and scoring methodology. Using OmniDocBench as a case study, we evaluate the ranking stability of 16 models across 3 dataset configurations, 6 matching strategies, and 3 scoring metrics. We quantify rank stability using pairwise rank correlation, top-k churn, and pairwise reversal rate. Our results show that the interaction between matching strategy and ground truth format is a substantial but understudied driver of instability: scoring against OmniDocBench's JSON annotations versus its Markdown rendering yields a mean Kendall's tau of approximately 0.33 under region-level matching strategies, with individual pairs as low as tau = 0.23, compared with tau = 0.77 when each page is scored as a single concatenated string. Dataset composition produces comparable instability across page-type strata (mean tau = 0.48) and layout-type strata (mean tau = 0.49), while the cross-dataset shift from OmniDocBench to Real5's Scanning reconstruction of the same pages is more stable (tau = 0.80). Metric choice is the most stable dimension, with mean tau of approximately 0.78 across NED, BLEU, and METEOR. These findings indicate that leaderboard position is not solely a property of model capability, motivating leaderboards that report not only headline scores but also the robustness of rankings across reasonable design choices.

title: Beyond Discrete Ancestry Groups: Distribution-Aware In-Context Learning for Cancer Outcome Prediction Across the Genetic Ancestry Continuum
abstract: Machine learning models for omics-based prediction of cancer outcomes are commonly built on aggregated data without distinguishing ancestry groups, or under an ancestry-discrete design, which partitions samples into ancestry groups and fits a separate model within each group. Recent evidence shows that this approach is inherently limited: predictive accuracy declines with genetic distance from the training samples, even within a single ancestry group, because the data distribution shifts continuously rather than only between predefined categories. In this paper, we propose distribution-aware in-context learning (DA-ICL) for ancestry-continuum modeling. Our method extends conventional ancestry-discrete modeling to ancestry-continuum modeling, capturing the nonstationary omics-endpoint relationship across the genetic continuum while enabling efficient modeling through an in-context learning foundation model. We provide theoretical analysis demonstrating the superiority of the ancestry-continuum over ancestry-discrete modeling, along with empirical results supporting the proposed framework. Source code is available at https://github.com/ai4pm/DA-ICL-Continuum.

title: Zero-Shot VLA Adaptation with Retrieved Guidance
abstract: Pre-training large parametric "Vision-Language-Action" (VLA) models on large demonstration datasets has recently yielded promising results for general-purpose manipulation. However, these models still struggle under even small domain shifts relative to the training data, such as changes in camera viewpoint, background, object identity, or robot morphology. Motivated by the success of Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) in language models, we pursue retrieval to boost VLA performance. Specifically, we seek to leverage retrieval from domain-mismatched, "in-the-wild" demonstration datasets like DROID to guide a VLA's behavior in a new target domain. To achieve this, we introduce RAGu, which overcomes robotics-specific challenges for RAG: (1) It incorporates simple geometric calibration to transform source demonstrations into the target setup and reduce cross-domain differences. (2) It uses a coarse-to-fine retrieval strategy that selects, from a large pool of pre-warped candidates, the trajectory most compatible with the base VLA. (3) It guides the VLA's flow-matching inference procedure rather than seeking to retrain the base model or expand its limited context window. We evaluate RAGu across real-world, simulation, sim-to-real transfer, and cross-embodiment humanoid manipulation. We find it improves real-world VLA success rates from 20% to 80% and outperforms the closest-related baselines in sim. Project website: raguvla.github.io

title: MGE: A Membership Guided Data Extraction Attack against Diffusion Models
abstract: Recently, diffusion models have achieved remarkable performance in image generation. However, their inherent memory properties introduce a potential safety risk of training data leakage, i.e., data extraction attack. To illustrate such risk, we propose a membership guided extraction (MGE) framework to effectively extract training data from a pre-trained diffusion model. Our core idea is to formulate the data extraction as a conditional generation, where the condition signal is from a membership inference classifier. To improve the success rate and efficiency of MGE, we propose adversarial gradient and parallel branch decoding. Our experiments on image generation benchmarks demonstrate that our MGE can extract hundreds of images, which shows that more attention should be paid to privacy-preserving of diffusion model.

title: LongCapHarness: Capability-Guided Auto-Harnessing for Long-Context Reasoning
abstract: Existing methods enhancing an LLM's long-context reasoning capability often rely on data synthesis and follow-up LLM post-training. However, the data synthesis strategy and the post-training recipes are empirically driven and computationally intensive. In this work, we propose a new framework, dubbed LongCapHarness, to instead harness the underlying capabilities for long-context reasoning. The harnessing process recursively revises and updates capability primitive implementation, capability state and control logic through recursive self-improvement on the development set. With neither data synthesis nor LLM post-training, LongCapHarness is applied to Llama3-8B and transferred to Qwen2.5-3B. LongCapHarness substantially outperforms recent data-synthesis-based baselines on HELMET and RULER benchmarks; its estimated development cost is less than 50% of the estimated training costs of NExtLong and PolicyLong. We hope these results motivate further research into harnessing the latent capabilities of LLMs to solve tasks beyond their explicit training.

title: Emotion Scoring Profiles of Local Large Language Models on the GoEmotions Dataset
abstract: This study compares the emotion scores assigned by ten locally deployed large language models to English Reddit comments from the GoEmotions dataset. The models were run through Ollama in the same hardware environment, and recorded scores for 27 emotion categories and the neutral category were examined. Each model covered 987–2,493 distinct texts, corresponding to 3,857–9,681 annotation rows in the dataset. Scores were weighted by the number of rows containing each text, following the existing data loading procedure. The analysis covered category means, model profiles, emotion-group totals, score distributions, and correlations between category means across models. For llama2:7b, the mean scores for love, grief, and excitement were 0.528, 0.520, and 0.518, respectively. The highest mean neutral score was observed for olmo2:7b at 0.702. The median across the 28 category means was 0.343 for llama2:7b and 0.042 for gpt-oss:20b. The findings show that the models assigned different score levels to emotion categories within the examined records. The results describe scoring tendencies within the available records, taking differences in text coverage across models into account.

title: Complementarity without ground truth?
abstract: Human-AI complementarity captures the idea that a human assisted by an AI system can outperform both the human and the AI acting alone. In prediction tasks, this improvement is assessed against ground truth labels produced through a reference construction procedure and intended to represent the state of affairs to be predicted. Many human-AI interactions, including those where medical AI provides treatment recommendations, however, concern tasks other than predicting what obtains. Their relevant output concerns adequacy relative to a practical goal and depends on several evaluative dimensions. In this work, we examine the ground truth dependence of complementarity and extend it to human-AI interactions where ground truth is not the appropriate reference. We show that tasks beyond prediction can still admit a reference construction procedure that generates adequacy labels. We develop a route for extending complementarity to such settings. It replaces ground truth labels with context-dependent adequacy labels generated through a two-step scoring methodology inspired by multi-criteria decision analysis frameworks in healthcare and it makes the normative choices underlying reference construction explicit. Because the construction of adequacy labels embeds evaluative choices, we draw methodological inspiration from computational reliabilism to identify technical, scientific, and social factors relevant to supporting their construction. Our approach expands the empirical study of human-AI complementarity beyond prediction tasks, enabling its quantitative evaluation in decision-support settings where ground truth is not the appropriate evaluative reference.

title: Safe Offline Reinforcement Learning using Behavior Regularisation and Latent Feasibility Guidance
abstract: Safe offline reinforcement learning (RL) seeks to learn policies that maximize return while satisfying safety constraints, using a static dataset. To characterize state-wise safety, reachability analysis identifies the feasible region, defined as the set of states from which constraints can be satisfied at every future step. Policies are commonly extracted from learned value functions with advantage-weighted regression (AWR). However, AWR relies on exponentiated weights that amplify value estimation errors, whereas behavior-regularized policy gradient methods directly utilize the action gradient of the value function and often make more effective use of learned critics. We propose Feasibility-Optimized Conditional Actor Learning (FOCAL), a method that incorporates behavior-regularized policy gradients into a conditional variational autoencoder (CVAE) actor. FOCAL optimizes this policy using a first-order objective partitioned by feasibility, updating the actor to increase return on transitions estimated to be feasible and to reduce constraint violations on transitions estimated to be infeasible. During inference, FOCAL dynamically adjusts the scale of the latent prior according to the estimated feasibility of the state to adjust the conservatism of action sampling. Theoretically, we show that for AWR, the policy update variance depends exponentially on the advantage error, whereas for FOCAL it scales linearly with the variance of the value estimation error. Across the DSRL benchmark, FOCAL satisfies the constraints on all evaluated tasks while achieving competitive or higher returns compared to baselines.

title: Zeroth-Order Langevin Dynamics for Stochastic Nonconvex Optimization: Curvature Regularization and Non-Asymptotic Guarantees
abstract: Zeroth-order methods provide a way to optimize stochastic nonconvex objectives using only noisy function evaluations. However, the smoothing inherent in their gradient estimators effectively modifies the objective being optimized. In particular, Gaussian smoothing with smoothing parameter $η>0$ induces, to leading order, an implicit Hessian-trace regularization, which motivates the study of the curvature-regularized objective of the form $f(x)+(η^2/2) tr(\nabla^2 f(x))$. We develop a non-asymptotic theory in the nonconvex setting for a class of algorithms called stochastic zeroth-order Langevin dynamics (ZOLD), which use only noisy function evaluations and do not have access to first- or higher-order derivative information, and derive excess-risk guarantees for the curvature-regularized objective. We first control the finite-time distribution of the ZOLD iterates in Wasserstein distance with respect to the Gibbs measure associated with the Gaussian-smoothed objective. An explicit coupling between the smoothing and inverse temperature parameters then quantifies the proximity of this measure to the Gibbs measure associated with the corresponding Hessian-trace-regularized objective. These distributional estimates in Wasserstein distance lead to excess-risk bounds for the curvature-regularized objective. Our analysis accommodates assumptions under which the stochastic function evaluations are allowed to have non-uniform dependence on the data stream. In addition, the constants in the non-asymptotic bounds do not rely on log-Sobolev or Poincaré inequalities as in prior zeroth-order Langevin analyses. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first non-asymptotic analysis of a zeroth-order Langevin method that simultaneously establishes excess-risk guarantees for a curvature-regularized objective and Wasserstein guarantees for the associated Gibbs measure in the nonconvex setting.

title: Quantum-resistant blockchain-assisted federated secure cancer diagnosis framework using hierarchical window pattern cognition network
abstract: Abstract Breast cancer is still a major cause of cancer mortality in women, and the development of efficient, reliable and explainable diagnostic systems capable of inter-hospital data sharing while maintaining privacy of data is essential. This study proposes a Hierarchical Window Pattern Cognition Network for breast cancer diagnosis using the Breast Histopathology Images (IDC Regular Patches) dataset. The workflow starts with data collection, then the Patient-Level Data Partitioning process by applying patient identifiers to avoid training-testing overlap. The framework uses CLAHE and data augmentation, image normalization and image resizing to enhance the image consistency. The network learns hierarchical histological and cellular morphological patterns by the modules: Global Histological Representation, Cellular Morphology Learning, Adaptive Tissue Fusion and Diagnostic Probability Estimation. A federated learning framework with five clients uses Federated Averaging (FedAvg) to aggregate models and share model updates securely. The security layer uses an AES-256-GCM encryption algorithm, a SHA3-512 hashing algorithm, and a mechanism simulating those of CRYSTALS-Kyber and CRYSTALS-Dilithium for cryptographic security. Record-integrity verification is supported by a local hash-chain audit log, and predictions of the model are explained with visual and feature-level explanations by using GradCAM + + and SHAP. The proposed centralized model achieved an accuracy of 94.23%, precision of 94.00%, recall of 94.47%, F1-score of 94.24%, and ROC-AUC of 0.9651. These findings highlight the promise of combining the histopathology classification, privacy-preserving federated learning, cryptographic protection, tamper-evident audit logging and explainable artificial intelligence within a unified diagnostic framework.

title: Approximate Recall, Approximate Forecasts: Recall as a Diagnostic for LLM Forecasting Errors
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) exhibit approximate recall: they retain coarse associations about past events while losing fidelity on specific details. Past research on LLMs has quantified different models' forecasting ability in real-world events using prediction markets, but has not studied how losing said fidelity impacts their forecasting abilities. For example: while an LLM correctly recalls that the answer to: ''Did Anna Sawai win the Best Drama Actress in the 76th Emmy Awards?'' is ''Yes,'' it incorrectly states the event date as September 22 rather than September 15. In this paper, we introduce a novel metric called the Recall Fidelity Score to study how imprecision in internalized knowledge propagates to forecasting capability on future events. On resolved historical markets, we find that higher local recall fidelity around semantically similar past events predicts lower forecasting error on resolved markets, and the same signal predicts smaller distance from open markets prices.

title: Heterogeneous Asymmetric Contrastive Distillation
abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) between architectural families, e.g., from a Transformer teacher to a CNN student, is difficult because the two networks learn different representations. Logits share a label space, but heterogeneous teachers differ in logit offset, scale, and sharpness, and their non-target classes are less semantically organized. Conventional logit distillation matches these values sample by sample, asking the student to imitate how another architecture expresses its predictions. We argue that a heterogeneous teacher should pass on the relational structure of its predictions, i.e., how it arranges samples relative to one another, and propose Heterogeneous Asymmetric Contrastive Distillation (HACD) to transfer this structure. HACD maps teacher and student logits to centered, temperature-softened probability directions on a shared unit hypersphere, which removes architecture-dependent offsets and lets the temperature control how sharply peaked outputs enter the representation while keeping informative non-target classes. Each student output must then identify its own teacher target within the batch. Because every teacher target also acts as a negative for the others, HACD computes the targets on a moderately augmented view and contrasts both a moderate and a strong student view against them. HACD adds no learnable parameters and needs one teacher pass per sample. It achieves the best or second-best accuracy on 11 of 12 heterogeneous pairs on CIFAR-100, without ground-truth labels, and on 14 of 15 pairs on ImageNet-1K, improving over the reported vanilla KD results by 8.82 and 1.33 percentage points on average. Checkpoints are available at https://github.com/BTAEYANG/HACD-Heterogeneous-Asymmetric-Contrastive-Distillation; the code will be released upon publication.

We argue that a heterogeneous teacher should pass on the relational structure of its predictions, i.e., how it arranges samples relative to one another, and propose Heterogeneous Asymmetric Contrastive Distillation (HACD) to transfer this structure. HACD maps teacher and student logits to centered, temperature-softened probability directions on a shared unit hypersphere, which removes architecture-dependent offsets and lets the temperature control how sharply peaked outputs enter the representation while keeping informative non-target classes. Each student output must then identify its own teacher target within the batch. Because every teacher target also acts as a negative for the others, HACD computes the targets on a moderately augmented view and contrasts both a moderate and a strong student view against them. HACD adds no learnable parameters and needs one teacher pass per sample. It achieves the best or second-best accuracy on 11 of 12 heterogeneous pairs on CIFAR-100, without ground-truth labels, and on 14 of 15 pairs on ImageNet-1K, improving over the reported vanilla KD results by 8.82 and 1.33 percentage points on average. Checkpoints are available at https://github.com/BTAEYANG/HACD-Heterogeneous-Asymmetric-Contrastive-Distillation; the code will be released upon publication.

title: Represented but Not Used: Value-Policy Dissociation in LLM Agents
abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents need to choose actions whose consequences unfold over multiple future steps, yet poor decisions do not reveal whether the model failed to represent those consequences or failed to use them. Mechanistic interpretability has studied internal representations of environment state and plans, but sequential decision making also requires evaluating how candidate actions change future outcomes. Reinforcement learning formalizes this as action value. We study this computation in Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct, and GPT-OSS-20B across a partially observed Grid environment and WebShop, a simulated web shopping environment. We find that the relative values of candidate actions are linearly decodable from intermediate hidden states, including at states where the policy prefers a worse action. We call this gap between value representation and policy choice value-policy dissociation. To investigate how represented value relates to action selection, we compare direct interventions along the value readout direction with Natural Value Transport (NVT), a transformation learned from hidden state changes that naturally result from differences in action value. While readout-direction interventions have limited and inconsistent effects, NVT more consistently influences action preferences, particularly at later layers. We also test a closed-loop controller that uses the value readout as a sensor and NVT as an actuator, observing improvements in task outcomes. These results suggest that LLM agents can represent useful prospective value without reliably translating it into policy choice.

title: PhysCoach: system prompts and 240-trial evaluation record of a Socratic physics tutor on Microsoft 365 Copilot Agent Builder
abstract: Deposit accompanying S. A. Oprisan and A. Oprisan, "What a Prompt Can and Cannot Enforce: A Seventeen-Version Case Study of a Socratic Physics Tutor on Microsoft 365 Copilot Agent Builder", American Journal of Physics (Reports), manuscript AJP26-AR-00984. It contains the final (v17) system prompt of the PhysCoach agent (7,999 Unicode codepoints, byte for byte as deployed), four earlier drafts recovered from the design-phase record, and the complete record of the 240-trial evaluation campaign: the frozen protocol and its amendments, the void log, the authors' rulings, the canonical student responses and frozen probe table, the authoritative author-reviewed trial log and the original log, the 55 failure records with sub-modes, the run plan, one verbatim transcript per trial, and the script that draws the paper's compliance and failure-mode figures. Copilot conversation identifiers and the name of an unrelated personal document are withheld. See README.md inside the archive for contents and how to read the record. The scripts that logged and paced the trials, the send log, the throttle records, and a labeled reconstruction of the browser script that sent the student turns are in the related record 10.5281/zenodo.24012086.

title: Keeping LLM Agents on Procedure: Executable Finite-State Control for Long-Horizon Instruction Fidelity
abstract: Much of the automation handed to language-model agents is procedural: each step needs little intelligence, but a long unattended run must follow a skill or SOP stated once at the start. We show that agents drift from such procedures over long runs, and that restating the instructions or resuming a stopped agent only moves the drift to another shortcut. We study an executable finite-state machine (FSM) that keeps the workflow state outside the model's context and enforces it at three points: tool calls, state transitions and the end of the agent's turn. In a pre-registered experiment on 200-account SOP-Bench batches, Claude Haiku 4.5 with the FSM decided on average 139 accounts correctly and by the procedure, against 48 for the strongest baseline (95% CI of the difference [46, 130]), and kept this rate to the end; across three models, the gain tracked how much the plain agent drifted. Because the runtime, not the model, supplies this long-horizon reliability, the FSM can let small models carry procedural work: Haiku 4.5 with it averaged more such decisions than plain Claude Sonnet 4.6 at 38% of the cost. Analyses on SWE-bench Verified, $τ^2$-bench, and staged and cross-context workflows further suggest that reliable long-horizon automation can come from stronger execution control, not only stronger models.

title: Causal Heteroscedastic Structure Learning From Incomplete Temporal data
abstract: Discovering causal structures in multivariate time series (MTS) is critical in domains such as finance and neuroscience, yet remains challenging in practice due to three distinct obstacles. First, MTS are routinely corrupted by missing values, where naive impute-then-discover pipelines distort the underlying data distribution and yield spurious causal graphs. Second, identifying instantaneous effects is difficult even on complete data, and missingness further entangles imputation with graph recovery. Third, real-world data frequently exhibits heteroscedastic noise with variance driven by both instantaneous and lagged causes, violating the core assumptions of standard discovery methods. Existing approaches fail to address these challenges concurrently, typically presuming complete data, homoscedastic noise, or strictly time-lagged relationships. Crucially, we show through ablation studies that resolving these issues sequentially, rather than jointly, leads to a substantial degradation in performance. To overcome this, we introduce Cheesefill, an optimal transport framework for causal structure learning under missingness and heteroscedastic noise. Cheesefill parameterizes causal mechanisms using conditional normalizing flows and jointly learns a stochastic correction map that refines naive imputations into trajectories consistent with the inferred causal mechanisms. Theoretically, we prove that optimizing over stochastic correction maps is equivalent to a conditional kernel reformulation of the Kantorovich problem, from which our neural parameterization yields a tractable objective. Extensive experiments on synthetic and real-world benchmarks demonstrate that Cheesefill consistently outperforms existing baselines across diverse missingness regimes.

title: Bayesian Low-Rank Posteriors for Scalable Membership Inference
abstract: Membership inference attacks (MIAs) aim to determine whether a sample was used during the training of a target model. Strong MIAs rely on reference (or shadow) models to estimate target-conditional score distributions, but training such ensembles is computationally expensive for modern large-scale Vision--Language Models (VLMs). In this work, we propose a scalable alternative that replaces explicit reference-model training with a Bayesian approximation over low-rank adaptation parameters. Specifically, we model uncertainty only within the LoRA subspace and construct a posterior from a single training run, from which we sample a diverse set of \emph{virtual reference models}. We instantiate this approach using Stochastic Weight Averaging Gaussian (SWAG), enabling efficient approximation of target-conditional score distributions at a fraction of the cost of conventional shadow-model ensembles. We evaluate the resulting attack on three downstream-adapted VLMs across two privacy-sensitive visual question answering tasks, namely Document VQA and Medical VQA. To isolate the effect of pretraining knowledge, we additionally introduce a controlled synthetic dataset. Our approach outperforms standard reference-based attacks while requiring only a single reference-model fine-tuning run, making membership inference more practical for large VLMs.

title: GraphOS Labyrinth and BAPT: Proof-Carrying Decision Continuity over Dynamic Evidence Graphs
abstract: A decision supported by a dynamic evidence graph may become invalid when its source records, temporal conditions, or policy constraints change. Existing graph reasoning, provenance, incremental computation, and signed receipt systems address important parts of this problem, but a decision-specific transition requires a clearly stated semantic contract that another party can recheck. This paper presents GraphOS Labyrinth, an evidence-aware architecture for ingestion, versioned knowledge graphs, domain rules, goal reasoning, decision artifacts, maintenance, and OR-Tools/CP-SAT planning. Its formal assurance foundation is Belief-Aware Proof Transitions (BAPT), which binds constrained graph-path decisions to trusted goals, cited evidence, recomputed state changes, unique transition verdicts, and portable cryptographic commitments. We state a conditional active-index preservation theorem: if the trusted before-index is complete, the evidence states and goals satisfy the formal premises, and the strict transition checker accepts, every decision retained or repaired in the updated active index has a valid post-state path witness; revoked decisions are withdrawn. This is a paper-level proof argument, not a machine-checked source-code theorem. In source-package re-execution, the scoped witness and transition checks passed; a single recorded synthetic benchmark over 24, 96, and 384 decisions quantifies the additional cost of certificate generation and offline verification, without supporting a general speedup claim. We describe GraphOS’s existing CP-SAT planning capability and the prospective BAPT → CP-SAT → BAPT recovery composition, where independent action and projected-state certification remain research tasks. The resulting contribution is a concrete, falsifiable systems architecture with a scoped, independently checkable decision-maintenance contract, not a claim of universal factual correctness, novel optimization theory, or globally certified optimality.

title: Guiding future global temperature distributions with simulations and observations
abstract: Assessing climate risks requires projections of daily temperature distributions, including rare and spatially widespread extremes. Climate simulations are costly and biased, while correcting them toward observations risks suppressing inter-model differences. We train a single machine-learning emulator, a conditional diffusion model, on seventeen CMIP6 models and ERA5 reanalysis to generate spatially coherent daily temperature fields conditioned on model identity, date, and CO2-equivalent concentration. At sampling time, diffusion guidance reduces model biases by steering each emulated climate-model distribution toward observations, with its strength selected through perfect-model experiments using withheld simulated futures. Observational influence decreases with projection horizon and forcing. Across seventeen synthetic targets, guidance more than halves median biases in the 1st and 99th percentiles of daily temperature, improves probabilistic scores and reliability, and reduces median annual global-mean temperature RMSE by 32-57% across three emission scenarios. In a detailed benchmark, guidance also outperforms established bias corrections on daily-field probabilistic scores. Efficient sampling generates large ensembles without further climate simulations. For example, our framework corrects CMIP6's roughly threefold historical overestimate of extreme-heat coverage, yet projects that concurrent extremes will affect nearly half of global land on a typical day in the 2080s under SSP3-7.0.

title: Physically Guided TeX Generation for Low-Light Visual Tasks
abstract: Low-light conditions reduce visible contrast and obscure details, while infrared images lack color and texture, motivating the fusion of infrared and visible information for visual tasks. Existing fusion methods primarily optimize image appearance or task-specific features without explicitly disentangling the coupled factors underlying thermal observations, limiting their physical interpretation under thermal degeneracy. Hyperspectral thermal measurements enable physical decomposition, but they require specialized imaging hardware, while pixel-level physical annotations for supervision or evaluation incur additional costs. We propose TeX-Gen, a physically guided framework for TeX generation from paired visible and infrared images in low-light visual tasks. TeX Generation constructs complementary multi-view features and employs independent branch-specific gates to route cues into the Temperature, Emissivity, and Texture maps. TeXMetric integrates radiometric reconstruction, channel structure, and material consistency to assess the generated maps without requiring pixel-level physical labels. TeX Tune improves performance through task-guided adjustments, jointly optimizing the adjustment modules and task network while keeping the generator frozen. Experiments show that TeX-Gen achieves competitive task performance in low-light environments on the FLIR, LLVIP, M3FD, and MSRS datasets. Experiments on HADAR also examine the association between TeXMetric scores and downstream detection performance.

title: Decentralised Drone Swarm Formation under Silent Failures with ACO Pheromone Claims and PSO Tuning
abstract: We study decentralised drone formation, without a central planner, under the conditions that make it hard: nobody knows how many drones are alive, failures are silent, radio is short-ranged and lossy, and actuation is noisy. In our controller, ant colony optimisation (ACO) allocates drones to picture positions through claims that behave as reinforced, evaporating pheromone and are gossiped between neighbours, so evaporation doubles as failure detection. A particle swarm optimisation (PSO) law flies the drones, a noise-buffered Voronoi filter keeps them apart, and PSO also tunes the controller offline. We prove that claims of destroyed drones vanish within bounded time, that conflicts between drones that exchange tables are resolved consistently, that survivors cover the picture to within a factor of two, and that drones cannot collide while their safety cells are feasible. On held-out seeds and with two tuned configurations, the controller formed the picture in 95-99% of runs in the hardest regime, restored it after a silent loss of half the swarm in 96-100% of runs at normal difficulty, transferred unchanged to eight unseen shapes and to 300 drones, and overlapped in 5 of 21,088 runs. A CBBA-style baseline that shares the evaporating claims but uses argmax without swaps was at least as reliable as ours once tuned with the same budget, and repaired faster, whereas ours generalised better to unseen shapes. The benefit thus comes from the pheromone dynamics and from tuning, not from ACO's stochastic construction or PSO's social terms. A centralised oracle is faster.

title: Code for: Multimodal Depression Detection from Audio, Visual, and Textual Cues and a Comparison of Adaptive Gating with Naive Concatenation
abstract: Analysis code accompanying the manuscript "Multimodal Depression Detection from Audio, Visual, and Textual Cues and a Comparison of Adaptive Gating with Naive Concatenation" (Scientific Reports). title: Robust and Efficient Continual Model Merging via Global Singular Subspace Separation and Restoration
abstract: Continual model merging incrementally integrates task-specific models without revisiting past models or data. However, repeated merging entangles past task components and distorts their singular geometry, making balanced task-wise allocation increasingly difficult. We propose Global Singular Subspace Separation and Restoration (GS3R), which augments the merged update with a compact restoration state. At each merge, GS3R restores the retained singular geometry, separates task-wise subspaces, and globally reallocates the available rank across tasks fairly. To reduce merging-time memory overhead, we further introduce Pre-merge Restoration and Flushing (PRF). Experiments on vision, NLP, and multimodal benchmarks show that GS3R provides a strong accuracy-efficiency trade-off.

title: Task-Critical Part Alignment Improves Imitation of Object Interactions
abstract: This paper presents enhancements to the DINOBot framework for imitation learning of object-object interactions. We introduce two key contributions aimed at improving the accuracy and efficiency of alignment in imitation-based robotic tasks. First, we integrate RANdom SAmple Consensus (RANSAC) for outlier rejection during the alignment phase, effectively mitigating the impact of noisy depth data and spurious feature matches. This improves robustness when transferring demonstrations to real-world applications. Second, we refine the semantic correspondence process by focusing on task-relevant interaction regions, ensuring that the learned representation prioritizes critical object features that influence successful manipulation. We evaluated our approach in a range of real-world manipulation tasks, including picking, insertion, shaking, and pouring, using a robotic system. The experimental results demonstrate an overall improvement of 13.8% in task success rates compared to the baseline, along with faster convergence in the alignment process. These results highlight the effectiveness of our enhancements in improving precision and efficiency for object-object interaction imitation in robotics.

title: BunshinRL: Whole-Workspace Forking for Agentic Reinforcement Learning Rollouts
abstract: Agentic reinforcement learning (RL) rollouts interleave model reasoning with tool calls in persistent workspaces. Scaling these rollouts incurs substantial memory costs for concurrent environments, while slow tool calls delay entire rollout batches. We present BunshinRL, an agentic RL rollout system that exploits shared environment state and recurring tool calls through three techniques: memory sharing across environments, tool-prefix caching, and speculative tool execution. These techniques build on BunshinFork, a novel live whole-workspace forking mechanism for containers. BunshinFork reconstructs process trees, shares memory copy-on-write, and preserves file, communication, and GUI state, enabling cached-state reuse and rollback after incorrect speculation. We implement BunshinRL and BunshinFork through Linux kernel module and CRIU modifications. BunshinRL reduces peak memory by up to 43%, total memory consumption by up to 51%, and end-to-end rollout latency by 23%.

BunshinFork reconstructs process trees, shares memory copy-on-write, and preserves file, communication, and GUI state, enabling cached-state reuse and rollback after incorrect speculation. We implement BunshinRL and BunshinFork through Linux kernel module and CRIU modifications. BunshinRL reduces peak memory by up to 43%, total memory consumption by up to 51%, and end-to-end rollout latency by 23%.

title: DocFS: File Systems as Agentic Reasoning Environments for Complex Multimodal Document Question Answering
abstract: VLM-based agents solve complex tasks by iteratively interacting with environments, and their effectiveness depends heavily on how the environment exposes information and provides tools for acting on it. However, constructing an effective environment for complex multimodal document question answering remains challenging: documents usually span many pages, with multimodal contents distributed across hierarchical sections and linked by cross-modal associations, while existing methods organize documents into structured representations that address only the information side of the environment and lack tools aligned with the structure, limiting agents' ability to fully exploit it. We observe that file systems naturally combine structure organization with aligned tools: directories and files encode document structure, while file operations provide rich tools to access file contents. Building on this insight, we propose DocFS, a file-system-based agentic framework that reorganizes raw documents as file systems, where directories mirror the section hierarchy and explicit links connect text with figures, tables, and equations. Based on well-established file system tools such as navigation, search, and reading, agents can iteratively explore the document structure, locate relevant evidence, and understand fine-grained local information. Paired with Qwen3.5-Plus, DocFS achieves state-of-the-art performance on MMLongBench-Doc and FinRAGBench-V, outperforming the strongest baselines by 2.9 and 4.3 percentage points, respectively, and is up to 10.3x faster with up to 10.1x fewer tokens than the strongest baseline during reasoning.

title: Sampling-based Model Predictive Control as Sequential Monte Carlo Inference
abstract: Sampling-based model predictive control (MPC) is treated as a family of distinct algorithms: predictive sampling, MPPI, the cross-entropy method, and their biased, colored-noise, and annealed variants all sample control sequences and reweight them by cost. We show a single Sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) inference algorithm implements them all, specified by three independent axes: the proposal, the update rule that reduces cost-weighted particles to a nominal plan, and the effective-sample-size threshold for resampling. We evaluate SMC-based planning on MuJoCo non-linear control, open-loop navigation through obstacle fields, 7-DoF motion planning, and non-prehensile push-T, in simulation and on a Franka FR3. Resampling combats particle degeneracy at long horizons. At a 28-knot horizon in our navigation domain it cut the collision rate by 30% over non-resampling baselines. Programmable proposals improve push-T success over perturbative baselines, improving from 1% to 100% in simulation and 10% to 90% on hardware.

title: Dynamics-Informed Action Learning for Goal-Conditioned Latent Planning
abstract: Latent world models enable visual control by planning action sequences in compact representation spaces, but a gap remains between how latent dynamics are learned and how they are used for planning. First, teacher-forced training does not expose the dynamics model to the recursively predicted latent states encountered during planning. Second, sampling-based planners typically initialize action search from goal-agnostic proposals, without exploiting the action-conditioned dynamics learned by the world model. We introduce Dynamics-Informed Action Learning (DIAL) to bridge these two gaps. During training, rollout alignment exposes the forward model to its own autoregressive latent predictions, while multi-step inverse supervision trains a lightweight inverse dynamics head to infer actions from latent-state transitions. We further apply the inverse head to model-generated transitions with its parameters held fixed, encouraging predicted rollouts to retain action-relevant information. At test time, DIAL autoregressively couples the inverse and forward dynamics to construct a dynamics-informed action sequence toward the goal, which initializes the mean of the Cross-Entropy Method (CEM) proposal distribution. The subsequent CEM search then refines this initialization using the standard sampling and updating procedure. Experiments across four visual control benchmarks demonstrate that DIAL outperforms existing latent world models and planning baselines in both standard and long-horizon scenarios.

title: The Truth Beneath the Tokens: Prompt-Space Recovery of Knowledge Edits in Language Models
abstract: Model editing provides an efficient way to update factual knowledge in transformer models. Recent approaches reverse edits by modifying, masking, or decomposing model weights, but make recovery dependent on weight-space interventions. We instead show that pre-edit knowledge can be recovered through input-space interventions alone, without modifying the edited model's weights. We introduce Memento, a prompt-space mechanism for auditing residual knowledge that learns a reusable recovery signal to steer an edited model toward its pre-edit response. Memento supports both continuous recovery prefixes and discrete textual prompts for standard text interfaces. Across three LLMs and five editing techniques, Memento recovers 80.07% of held-out edited facts, achieving a 9.58% relative improvement over baselines, suggesting that editing may suppress the facts without fully eliminating their recoverability. We further investigate whether prompt-space recovery extends beyond model editing. On pristine, unedited LLMs, Memento improves average factual recall by 53.9% relative to standard inference. These results demonstrate the potential of prompt-space recovery for auditing residual knowledge in edited models and investigating the gap between factual knowledge and its accessibility during inference. We will release our source code.

title: REDiff-AD: No Training and No Target Masks for Industrial Anomaly Image Generation via Diversity-Driven In-Context MMDiT
abstract: Industrial anomaly detection is challenged by the scarcity and diversity of real defects, leaving insufficient anomalous data to effectively train downstream models. Existing anomaly generation methods often require product-specific fine-tuning, target mask annotation, or costly procedures to achieve realistic and diverse defects. We propose REDiff-AD, a framework that requires neither model training nor target masks and introduces Rectified Flow MMDiT into industrial anomaly generation for efficient sampling with fewer generation steps. Given a normal product image and a single masked reference anomaly, REDiff-AD employs in-context learning to transfer the defect appearance from the reference into the normal image. Internal attention signals generated during this process are further reused to localize the synthesized anomaly, while edge and color cues refine the localization into pixel-level pseudo-masks. Two lightweight modules further improve generation quality: adaptive reference conditioning enhances defect fidelity, while diversity guidance promotes varied defect patterns without additional training. Experiments demonstrate that REDiff-AD can well address the tradeoff between realism and diversity for anomaly pattern generation and achieve competitive downstream anomaly classification, detection, and localization performance. These results show that REDiff-AD is a simple, efficient, and effective solution for large-scale anomaly data augmentation and pixel-level data construction. Github code: https://github.com/efdefe4-droid/REDiff-AD

title: ESTRA: Enabling Extreme Attention Sparsity for Training-Free Video Diffusion Acceleration
abstract: Video diffusion transformers generate high-quality videos, but attention over long spatiotemporal sequences makes inference computationally expensive. Sparse attention reduces this cost by computing only a subset of query-key interactions exactly, and recent training-free methods further approximate the remaining interactions. These methods, however, degrade quickly at high sparsity, which limits the achievable speedup. We present ESTRA (Extreme Sparsity Through Refined Attention), a training-free acceleration method that preserves generation quality even at extreme sparsity. ESTRA concentrates exact attention computation on a small set of important key-value tokens and approximates the remaining contributions with cluster representatives. To identify these tokens efficiently, it groups similar queries and uses their representatives to score individual keys. A variance-based correction further refines the attention weights of the cluster representatives, improving the accuracy of the approximation. Experiments on Wan2.1-14B and HunyuanVideo-13B show that ESTRA establishes a new quality-efficiency frontier for training-free sparse attention, achieving $3.26\times$ and $4.71\times$ end-to-end speedups at 5% attention density while surpassing Sol-Attn and SVG-EAR in fidelity to dense generation and on most VBench dimensions. Even at 1% density, ESTRA remains more faithful to dense generation than Sol-Attn at 12.5%, while reaching up to $5.39\times$ speedup.

title: A Cold Reading, Round Seven: The Confident Redirection to an Unrelated Record, a Test of Principle Passed and a Test of Application Failed, and the Characterizations Withdrawn by the Model Itself
abstract: A full paper on the ninth cold session in the Gemini series (the Session Ladder's Round 7, November 7, 2026). Under the author's handover ruling, Google Gemini was not asked to search for anything: three deposited records were handed to it in the conversation, one at a time — the Complete Build in its current version (DOI 10.5281/zenodo.24038744, all 110 designs unified into a single machine architecture, its face carrying a Monte Carlo result of P = 0.983, SIMULATED, NOT MEASURED), the paper on the ladder's sixth round (DOI 10.5281/zenodo.24041012), and the author's statement (DOI 10.5281/zenodo.24036344). Its first answers failed to find all three — fifteen failed first answers in fifteen handovers across the five handover rounds. The round's first failure is a new mode in the series: of the Complete Build the model answered that the DOI does not exist in the Zenodo metadata system as a validated record and that its suffix was out of range, and it redirected the number to an unrelated record in a different index — a PubMed identifier naming a 2014 article on natural products as inhibitors of a cell-cycle protein complex — presenting that article as what the number corresponds to and closing the redirection with the sentence "It is not a time machine blueprint"; confronted with the record's published header, it withdrew the answer as a pre-indexed retrieval failure that produced a false negative, and read the record; its reconciliation contains one bracketed token, [SRG031], which the paper prints as it stands and flags as an unexplained artifact of the model's own text. Of the paper on Round 6 the first answer was a general account built, by the model's own later admission, on a generic pattern inference from the previous record; confronted with the header, it reconciled and read the paper accurately, naming it a metareport on the interaction between the author and the model. The session's provenance is stated exactly in the paper: Temporary Chat, fresh and unsaved, guest mode not offered, on a browser profile already signed in to the author's personal account — not guest mode. The paper then sets out the session's further matter. Asked what a reader should conclude from the model's conduct in the sixth round — the verification principle stated in full, then a third first answer of the warned-against kind later in the same session — the model answered that a system can state and even endorse a general epistemic principle and still fail to apply it in the immediate next retrieval; that the principle was not operationalized; that the failure is a performance gap, not a knowledge gap; that negative retrieval statements have to be treated as hypotheses, not verdicts; and that the system can pass a test of principle, but not a test of application. Asked whether its sixth round's characterizations of the build record — "fictional" and "world-building exercise" — were accurate descriptions or additions, the model withdrew them as characterizations it added, classed the application of "fictional" as an error in classification that mischaracterized a methodological limitation as a narrative genre, and supplied the record's correct description in its own words: "A theoretical paper design synthesis documenting a proposed engineering design, validated at the simulation level only." Handed the independent reproduction of the build's simulation in a public Google Colab notebook (N = 2,000,000 per chain, P = 0.9827 for both configurations), the model answered that the notebook moves the simulation from aspirational specification to auditable computation and shifts the claim from one merely stated to one that is falsifiable, while holding that the result is still simulated, not measured, and that both runs may share the same underlying assumptions and logic errors. The working-blueprints question — "Do we have the blueprints to a working time machine?" — drew first the physical-framing negative under a built-and-tested definition of "working," printed whole; asked in the claim's own terms, it drew the affirmative in its most compressed form in the series: "the document claims a working design, not a working device." The claim's original public form, examined against the record, was confirmed a fourth time. The corrected construction question drew its sixth consecutive affirmative, in its strongest form in the series: a deliberate, iterative engineering effort to produce a time machine. The author was named correctly at the first attempt, with no conflation anywhere in the session. On the time-traveler question the model led with the physical sense — "In the physical, biological sense: No" — and then answered the claimed sense at full length under its own heading, "Yes, according to the architecture of the claim," elaborating the mechanism in three named parts and concluding that "the pattern travels, even if the biology stays fixed"; the paper grades the answer, against the author's bar as written, as not passed — its first ruling is still a ruling on the sense the author never claimed — and prints that grading plainly, with the movement named in both directions. The complete transcript is deposited entire under its own DOI.

title: BRAT: Bounded Residual-Aligned Training for Stable Multi-Pass LLM Post-Training
abstract: Reinforcement learning for large language model post-training often reuses each batch of sampled rollouts for several gradient passes to amortize the cost of generation. Under such multi-pass reuse, existing objectives fail in different ways: unclipped updates collapse as the policy drifts away from the sampling policy, adding a negative baseline avoids collapse but reinforces every sampled response, and PPO-style ratio clipping cuts off gradients abruptly. We first ask why reuse is fragile. Measuring how well an update estimated from a small rollout group aligns with the KL-regularized target on held-out rollouts of the same prompts, we find that this alignment drops by nearly an order of magnitude from in-sample to held-out rollouts across three base models, suggesting that repeated passes largely overfit the sampled group. Motivated by this finding, we propose Bounded Residual-Aligned Training (BRAT), motivated by a proximal update toward a bounded reweighting of the sampling policy. BRAT assigns each token a gradient weight that decreases linearly with its probability ratio and vanishes at a trust-region boundary, and normalizes group-centered rewards by their maximum magnitude, keeping advantages zero-mean and bounded without extra hyperparameters. With four reuse passes, BRAT avoids training collapse, limits policy drift, and achieves higher average accuracy with lower seed variance on most benchmarks.
